subject: science
title: Chemistry — Materials
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Chemistry — Materials, KS3 Science (National Curriculum).
meta_desc: KS3 Science practice covering Chemistry — Materials, from the National Curriculum programme of study.
final_note: You worked through Chemistry — Materials: 3 programme-of-study statements.

concepts.def: A list of metals in order of how readily they react, with the most reactive at the top. The KS3 order is: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, lead, copper, silver, gold. Carbon is a non-metal, but it is placed in the list because its position shows which metals it can extract.
concepts.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series

concepts.def: A reactive metal reacts quickly and strongly with water, dilute acids and oxygen (potassium and sodium react fast even with cold water). An unreactive metal reacts slowly or not at all (copper, silver and gold do not react with water, dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulfuric acid). The faster the bubbling or the more vigorous the reaction, the higher the metal is in the series.
concepts.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series

concepts.def: Metals are put in order by comparing how they react under the same conditions: same-sized pieces in cold water, or in the same dilute acid. More bubbles, more heat or a faster reaction means a more reactive metal.
concepts.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series

concepts.def: A rock that contains enough of a metal compound (often the metal oxide) to make it worth extracting the metal. Only a few very unreactive metals, such as gold, are found in the ground as the pure metal.
concepts.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides

concepts.def: A compound of a metal and oxygen, such as iron oxide or copper oxide. The metal and oxygen are chemically joined, not just mixed, so a chemical reaction is needed to separate them: heating iron oxide or copper oxide on its own does not give the metal.
concepts.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides

concepts.def: Getting a metal out of its compound in an ore. For a metal oxide, the oxygen must be removed by a chemical reaction.
concepts.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides

concepts.def: At KS3: loss of oxygen. When carbon takes the oxygen from a metal oxide, the metal oxide is reduced and the metal is left. In science 'reduced' does not mean made smaller.
concepts.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides

concepts.def: At KS3: gain of oxygen. When carbon takes oxygen from a metal oxide, the carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide. Reduction and oxidation happen together.
concepts.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides

concepts.def: A metal below carbon in the reactivity series (zinc, iron, lead, copper) can be extracted by heating its oxide strongly with carbon. Carbon is more reactive than the metal, so it takes the oxygen: metal oxide + carbon → metal + carbon dioxide (for example, iron oxide + carbon → iron + carbon dioxide). Metals above carbon (potassium to aluminium) cannot be extracted this way.
concepts.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides

concepts.def: A method that uses electricity to split a compound. It is used to extract metals that are above carbon in the reactivity series, such as aluminium. How it works is GCSE content.
concepts.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides

concepts.def: A hard material made by heating clay or sand to a very high temperature, such as pottery, china, bricks and glass. Ceramics are hard and stiff, stay solid at very high temperatures and do not conduct electricity, but they are brittle.
concepts.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)

concepts.def: A substance made of very long chain molecules. Plastics are polymers, and most plastics are made from crude oil. Polymers are usually light, easy to mould into shape, waterproof and good insulators of electricity and heat; many are flexible, some are hard and stiff, and most soften or melt when heated.
concepts.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)

concepts.def: A material made by combining two or more materials so that it has properties none of them has alone. It has a matrix (the material that holds it together) and a reinforcement (fibres or lumps) spread through it. Examples: fibreglass (glass fibres in a plastic), carbon fibre (carbon fibres in a plastic), concrete (stones and sand in cement), reinforced concrete (steel rods in concrete).
concepts.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)

concepts.def: Hard to scratch or dent. A hard material is not always hard to break: a ceramic tile is hard but can shatter.
concepts.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)

concepts.def: Breaks or shatters suddenly, without bending first, when hit or bent. Ceramics such as glass and pottery are brittle.
concepts.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)

concepts.def: Hard to break when hit or bent: a tough material bends or dents instead of shattering. The opposite of brittle.
concepts.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)

concepts.def: A stiff material is hard to bend; a flexible material bends easily. Ceramics are stiff; many polymers are flexible.
concepts.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)

concepts.def: An electrical insulator does not let electricity pass through it; a heat (thermal) insulator lets heat pass through only slowly. Polymers and ceramics are good insulators. Metals are good conductors of electricity and of heat.
concepts.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)

concepts.def: List what the job needs (for example light, stiff, waterproof, does not shatter, stays solid when hot), then pick the material whose properties match all of these needs, not just one of them.
concepts.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)

mcqs.q: In the reactivity series, where is carbon placed?
options: Below gold, at the bottom
Between aluminium and zinc
Above potassium, at the top
Between iron and copper
mcqs.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
mcqs.explain: Yes. Carbon sits below aluminium and above zinc. Potassium to aluminium are more reactive than carbon; zinc to gold are less reactive.
rationales: You may have thought carbon goes after all the metals because it is a non-metal. In fact carbon sits among them, below aluminium and above zinc.
Yes. Carbon sits below aluminium and above zinc. Potassium to aluminium are more reactive than carbon; zinc to gold are less reactive.
You may have thought carbon can take oxygen from any metal, so it must be at the top. In fact carbon is less reactive than potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium and aluminium.
You may have thought carbon marks the point where metals stop reacting with acid. In fact zinc and iron are below carbon and still react; carbon sits between aluminium and zinc.

mcqs.q: A piece of zinc and a piece of copper are put into separate test tubes of dilute hydrochloric acid. What would you see?
options: Only the zinc gives bubbles
Only the copper gives bubbles
Both metals give bubbles
No bubbles on either metal
mcqs.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
mcqs.explain: Yes. Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series and reacts with the acid, so it fizzes. Copper is too unreactive to react with dilute acid.
rationales: Yes. Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series and reacts with the acid, so it fizzes. Copper is too unreactive to react with dilute acid.
You may have thought copper is more reactive because copper roofs and statues slowly turn green. In fact zinc is higher in the series: zinc fizzes and copper does not.
You may have thought an acid eats away any metal. In fact copper is too low in the series to react with dilute acid, so only the zinc fizzes.
You may have thought the metals below carbon do not react at all. In fact zinc still reacts with dilute acid and fizzes; copper does not.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the reactivity series is correct?
options: Iron is more reactive than sodium
Iron is more reactive than aluminium
Calcium is more reactive than iron
Copper is more reactive than carbon
mcqs.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
mcqs.explain: Yes. Calcium is near the top of the series, above carbon, while iron is below carbon, so calcium is much more reactive.
rationales: You may have thought iron is more reactive because it is hard and strong, while sodium is soft. In fact reactivity is not hardness: sodium is near the top of the series.
You may have thought aluminium is unreactive because it does not rust. In fact aluminium is above iron; a thin oxide coat on its surface protects it.
Yes. Calcium is near the top of the series, above carbon, while iron is below carbon, so calcium is much more reactive.
You may have thought carbon goes below all the metals because it is a non-metal. In fact carbon is above copper, which is why carbon can take oxygen from copper oxide.

mcqs.q: Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water. Which element reacts faster than magnesium with cold water?
options: Iron (Fe)
Carbon (C)
Copper (Cu)
Calcium (Ca)
mcqs.specStatementText: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
mcqs.explain: Yes. Calcium is above magnesium in the reactivity series, so it reacts faster: it bubbles steadily in cold water.
rationales: You may have thought iron is more reactive because it is a hard, strong metal. In fact iron is below magnesium in the series and gives no bubbles in cold water.
You may have thought carbon is above every metal because it extracts metals. In fact carbon is below magnesium and does not react with cold water.

You may have thought copper reacts with water because copper roofs turn green in the rain. In fact that green coat forms over many years; copper is near the bottom of the series and does not react with cold water.
Yes. Calcium is above magnesium in the reactivity series, so it reacts faster: it bubbles steadily in cold water.

mcqs.q: Copper oxide powder is heated strongly with carbon powder. What does the carbon do?
options: It takes the oxygen from the copper oxide
It burns to make heat that frees the copper
It joins on to the copper to make a compound
It destroys all the oxygen in the copper oxide
mcqs.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
mcqs.explain: Yes. Carbon is more reactive than copper, so it takes the oxygen and becomes carbon dioxide: copper oxide + carbon → copper + carbon dioxide.
rationales: Yes. Carbon is more reactive than copper, so it takes the oxygen and becomes carbon dioxide: copper oxide + carbon → copper + carbon dioxide.
You may have thought carbon is only a fuel. In fact heating copper oxide on its own does not give copper; the carbon reacts and takes the oxygen.
You may have thought the carbon combines with the copper. In fact the carbon joins with the oxygen, leaving copper on its own.
You may have thought the oxygen disappears. In fact no oxygen is destroyed: it joins with carbon to make carbon dioxide gas, which you cannot see.

mcqs.q: In a furnace, iron oxide is heated strongly with carbon. What are the products?
options: Iron carbonate alone
Iron and oxygen gas
Iron and nothing else
Iron and carbon dioxide
mcqs.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
mcqs.explain: Yes. Carbon takes the oxygen from the iron oxide: iron oxide + carbon → iron + carbon dioxide.
rationales: You may have thought the carbon joins the iron to make a carbonate. In fact the carbon joins with the oxygen, so iron is left on its own and carbon dioxide forms.
You may have thought the heat splits iron oxide into iron and oxygen. In fact the oxygen leaves joined to carbon, as carbon dioxide.
You may have thought the oxygen and carbon are burnt away. In fact no atoms are destroyed: they leave together as carbon dioxide gas.
Yes. Carbon takes the oxygen from the iron oxide: iron oxide + carbon → iron + carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: Lead is less reactive than iron but more reactive than copper. Which statement about getting lead from lead oxide is correct?
options: Carbon can extract it, as carbon extracts any metal
Carbon can extract it, as lead is below carbon
Carbon cannot extract it, as carbon is below lead
Carbon cannot extract it, as lead is unreactive
mcqs.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
mcqs.explain: Yes. Lead is below iron, so it is below carbon too. Carbon is more reactive, so it takes the oxygen: lead oxide + carbon → lead + carbon dioxide.
rationales: You may have thought carbon works for every metal. Carbon does extract lead, but only because lead is below carbon; it cannot extract metals above it, such as aluminium.
Yes. Lead is below iron, so it is below carbon too. Carbon is more reactive, so it takes the oxygen: lead oxide + carbon → lead + carbon dioxide.
You may have thought carbon goes below all the metals because it is a non-metal. In fact carbon is above zinc and iron, so it is above lead too and can take lead oxide's oxygen.
You may have thought less reactive metals are harder to extract. In fact it is the other way round: lead is below carbon, so carbon can take its oxygen.

mcqs.q: Zinc oxide is heated with carbon, and the zinc oxide is reduced. In chemistry, what does 'reduced' mean?
options: It has gained oxygen
It has become smaller
It has lost its oxygen
It has joined to carbon
mcqs.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
mcqs.explain: Yes. At KS3, reduction is loss of oxygen. Carbon takes the oxygen, so zinc is left.
rationales: You may have mixed up reduction and oxidation. Gaining oxygen is oxidation; it is the carbon that gains oxygen here.
You may have used the everyday meaning of 'reduced'. In chemistry it means losing oxygen; the solid does get lighter, but only because its oxygen has gone.
Yes. At KS3, reduction is loss of oxygen. Carbon takes the oxygen, so zinc is left.
You may have thought the carbon joins on to the zinc. In fact the carbon joins the oxygen and leaves as carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows part of the reactivity series, with a new metal, X. How would metal X most likely be obtained?
options: By heating X oxide with carbon
By heating X oxide on its own
By digging up pure X from rocks
By electrolysis of a compound of X
mcqs.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
mcqs.explain: Yes. X is above carbon, so carbon cannot take the oxygen from X oxide. Metals above carbon are extracted another way, such as electrolysis.
rationales: You may have thought carbon can extract any metal. In fact X is above carbon in the diagram, so carbon cannot take its oxygen.
You may have thought heat alone frees a metal from its oxide. In fact heating the oxide of a metal as reactive as X does not remove the oxygen; X is too reactive even for carbon.
You may have thought metals are found as the pure metal. In fact a metal as reactive as X is always found joined to other elements in compounds.
Yes. X is above carbon, so carbon cannot take the oxygen from X oxide. Metals above carbon are extracted another way, such as electrolysis.

mcqs.q: In a furnace, zinc oxide and aluminium oxide are each heated strongly with carbon. Which metal is made?
options: Zinc, but not aluminium
Aluminium, but not zinc
Both zinc and aluminium
Neither of these metals
mcqs.specStatementText: the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
mcqs.explain: Yes. Zinc is below carbon, so carbon takes the oxygen from zinc oxide. Aluminium is above carbon, so carbon cannot take its oxygen.
rationales: Yes. Zinc is below carbon, so carbon takes the oxygen from zinc oxide. Aluminium is above carbon, so carbon cannot take its oxygen.
You may have thought a more reactive metal is easier to extract. In fact it is harder: carbon cannot take oxygen from aluminium oxide.
You may have thought carbon can extract any metal. In fact carbon only works for metals below it, so aluminium is not made.
You may have thought carbon is below all the metals. In fact carbon is above zinc, so it can take the oxygen from zinc oxide.

mcqs.q: Which statement about materials is correct?
options: Metals are very good heat insulators
A kettle case is too hard to be a polymer
Ceramics are hard but can shatter
Carbon fibre is light and so it is weak
mcqs.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
mcqs.explain: Yes. Ceramics are hard and stiff, but they are brittle, so a mug or tile can crack or shatter when dropped.
rationales: You may have thought metal flasks keep drinks hot because metal insulates. In fact metals are good heat conductors; the flask works because of a vacuum.
You may have thought all plastics are soft and bendy. In fact some polymers are hard and stiff: kettle cases and plugs are made of them.
Yes. Ceramics are hard and stiff, but they are brittle, so a mug or tile can crack or shatter when dropped.
You may have thought light materials must be weak. In fact carbon fibre is light but strong, which is why it is used for bike frames.

mcqs.q: Which of these statements is correct?
options: Tiles are so hard that they do not crack
Plastic bottles soften when heated
Foam insulates, so it stays solid in a fire
Fibreglass shatters just like glass
mcqs.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
mcqs.explain: Yes. Plastic bottles are made of a polymer, and most polymers soften or melt when heated. That is why plastic is not used for very hot jobs.
rationales: You may have thought very hard means hard to break. In fact ceramic tiles are hard but brittle, so they can crack or shatter when something hits them.
Yes. Plastic bottles are made of a polymer, and most polymers soften or melt when heated. That is why plastic is not used for very hot jobs.
You may have thought a heat insulator must stand great heat. In fact polystyrene foam is a good insulator but melts and burns at quite low temperatures.
You may have thought a composite keeps the properties of each part. In fact the plastic holds the glass fibres, so fibreglass does not shatter like glass.

mcqs.q: A kiln heats pottery to over 1000 °C. Which material is best for lining the inside of the kiln?
options: A ceramic, as it stays solid when very hot
A polymer, as it is a good heat insulator
A metal, as it is a good heat insulator
Fibreglass, as it has the properties of glass
mcqs.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
mcqs.explain: Yes. Ceramics stay solid at very high temperatures and let heat through only slowly, so they are used to line kilns and furnaces.
rationales: Yes. Ceramics stay solid at very high temperatures and let heat through only slowly, so they are used to line kilns and furnaces.
You may have thought a good insulator can stand great heat. In fact polymers soften, melt or burn far below 1000 °C.
You may have thought metals insulate. In fact metals are good heat conductors, so a metal lining would let heat escape.
You may have thought a composite has every property of its parts. In fact the plastic in fibreglass would soften and burn at kiln temperatures.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows fibreglass: thin glass fibres held in a plastic. Compared with a sheet of glass, fibreglass is …
options: weaker, because it is lighter than glass
just as soft and bendy as plastic
better for hot jobs as it insulates
much less likely to shatter when hit
mcqs.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
mcqs.explain: Yes. The plastic holds the fibres and stops cracks spreading, so fibreglass is tough, while a glass sheet is brittle.
rationales: You may have thought a lighter material must be weaker. In fact fibreglass is light and strong; that is why boats are made of it.
You may have thought anything containing plastic is soft and bendy. In fact the glass fibres make fibreglass stiff and strong.
You may have thought a heat insulator can stand great heat. In fact the plastic in fibreglass softens when hot, while glass does not.
Yes. The plastic holds the fibres and stops cracks spreading, so fibreglass is tough, while a glass sheet is brittle.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows reinforced concrete: steel rods inside concrete. Concrete on its own cracks easily when it is bent. What do the steel rods do?
options: Nothing, as it is just a mixture
They stop it snapping when it bends
They make it so hard it cannot crack
They keep heat out, as metals insulate
mcqs.specStatementText: properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
mcqs.explain: Yes. Concrete is strong when squashed but cracks when bent; the steel rods hold it together, so the composite does not snap.
rationales: You may have thought the parts just keep their own properties. In fact the rods and concrete work together, giving a material that resists bending.
Yes. Concrete is strong when squashed but cracks when bent; the steel rods hold it together, so the composite does not snap.
You may have thought hardness stops cracking. In fact the rods do not make the concrete harder; they stop it snapping when bent.
You may have thought metals are heat insulators. In fact metals conduct heat well; the rods are there to stop the concrete snapping.

specStatements.text: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)

scopeNotes.decision: The order tested is potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, lead, copper, silver, gold (most reactive first), including carbon's place between aluminium and zinc; the order is also used to predict and explain what is seen when metals are put in cold water or dilute acid.
scopeNotes.basis: The key stage 3 programme of study names 'the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series'. Hydrogen's place in the series, displacement reactions and reactions with oxygen belong to the key stage 3 heading 'Chemical reactions' or to GCSE (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item, concept or rationale uses hydrogen's place in the series, and no item asks about a displacement reaction. No item asks the student to recall where lead goes, because the site's lesson leaves lead out of its list: the one item about lead gives its position in the stem (below iron, above copper).

scopeNotes.decision: Carbon extracts a metal below it in the reactivity series by taking the oxygen from the metal oxide (the metal oxide is reduced, which means it loses oxygen); a metal above carbon must be extracted another way, and electrolysis is named as that way only.
scopeNotes.basis: How electrolysis works (electrodes, ions, half equations), reduction and oxidation as electron transfer and the reactions inside a blast furnace (carbon monoxide, limestone, slag) are GCSE content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Electrolysis appears only as a name, in one option and its rationale, two misconception cards and one concept card; no item, concept or rationale mentions electrodes, ions, electrons, carbon monoxide or slag. Every equation is a word equation, and reduction and oxidation are defined only as loss and gain of oxygen.

scopeNotes.decision: Ceramics, polymers and composites are tested through their typical properties (hard, brittle, stiff, flexible, tough, light, heat-resistant, electrical and heat insulators), described in words, and through choosing a material for a job.
scopeNotes.basis: The statement says '(qualitative)'. The structure of polymer chains and how polymers are made (polymerisation) are GCSE content (DfE, GCSE chemistry subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item gives a number for a property of a material (the only number is the working temperature of a pottery kiln, over 1000 °C), and no item shows or asks about the structure of a polymer chain or how polymers are made. The words 'very long chain molecules' appear only in the polymer concept card, to match the site's lesson.
